instruction: What is the difference between culpable homicide and murder in Indian criminal law?
response: The distinction between culpable homicide (Section 299 IPC) and murder (Section 300 IPC) is one of degree of probability of death. As held by Melvill J. in Reg v. Govinda and reiterated by the Supreme Court, all murder is culpable homicide, but not all culpable homicide is murder. Culpable homicide involves an intention or knowledge that death is 'likely' to result, whereas murder involves an intention or knowledge of 'imminent danger' where death is the most probable and almost certain consequence.

instruction: Explain the legal significance of Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act.
response: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act operates as an exception to Sections 25 and 26 (which bar confessions made to police). It embodies the doctrine of confirmation by subsequent facts. When any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from an accused in police custody, so much of that information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered, may be proved. The discovered object and the place of recovery must be distinctly linked to the disclosure.

instruction: What remedies are available against an order of rejection of bail by a Sessions Court?
response: When a Sessions Court rejects a regular bail application under Section 439 CrPC, the accused has the concurrent statutory remedy to approach the High Court under Section 439 of the CrPC for the grant of bail. If the High Court also rejects bail, the accused may approach the Supreme Court by filing a Special Leave Petition (Criminal) under Article 136 of the Constitution of India. Successive bail applications can only be maintained before the same court if there is a substantial, material change in circumstances.

instruction: Under what circumstances can a criminal appeal against acquittal be entertained by the High Court?
response: An appeal against acquittal is governed by Section 378 CrPC. While the High Court has full power to review and re-weigh the evidence, it exercises this jurisdiction with great caution. The presumption of innocence is reinforced by an order of acquittal. As held in Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka (2007), the High Court will interfere with an acquittal only if the trial court's judgment is perverse, palpably erroneous, based on erroneous view of law, or where vital evidence was ignored, and not merely because another reasonable view was possible.

instruction: What is the effect of non-compliance with Section 50 of the NDPS Act?
response: Section 50 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 mandates that when an authorized officer is about to search any person, they must inform the person of their legal right to be taken without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer or Magistrate for search. In Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja (2011), the Constitution Bench held that informing the suspect of this right is mandatory and strict compliance is obligatory. Failure to do so vitiates the recovery of contraband from the person, rendering the conviction unsustainable.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Constructive Res Judicata' under Explanation IV to Section 11 CPC.
response: Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure codifies 'Constructive Res Judicata'. It provides that any matter which might and ought to have been made ground of defence or attack in a former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. Even if a party omitted to raise a plea which was available to them, they are precluded from raising it in subsequent litigation between the same parties, preventing endless multiplicity of proceedings.

instruction: What are the requirements for invoking the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution?
response: Article 227 of the Constitution confers power of superintendence upon High Courts over all subordinate courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction. It is an administrative as well as judicial supervisory power. As held in Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil (2010), this power is exercised sparingly, only to keep subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority, and not as an appellate power to correct mere errors of fact or law.

instruction: Explain the scope and nature of Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
response: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 enables a party to apply to a court for interim measures of protection before, during arbitral proceedings, or after the making of the arbitral award but before it is enforced under Section 36. Reliefs include preservation, custody, sale of goods, interim injunctions, and appointment of a receiver. If interim relief is granted prior to arbitral proceedings, arbitration must be commenced within 90 days under Section 9(2).

instruction: What is the evidentiary requirement for proving a Will under Section 68 of the Evidence Act?
response: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act read with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, a Will must be attested by two or more witnesses, each of whom must have seen the testator sign or affix their mark. To prove a Will, at least one attesting witness who is alive and capable of giving evidence must be examined in court. The propounder must also dispel any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the Will.

instruction: Explain the difference between Legal Set-Off under Order VIII Rule 6 CPC and Equitable Set-Off.
response: Under Order VIII Rule 6 CPC, a Legal Set-Off requires: (1) an ascertained sum of money; (2) legally recoverable; (3) both parties filling the same character; and (4) court having pecuniary jurisdiction. In contrast, an Equitable Set-Off arises when cross-demands arise out of the very same transaction or series of transactions so connected that it would be inequitable to drive the defendant to a separate suit, even if the amount is unascertained.

instruction: What is the legal position regarding the admissibility of CDR (Call Detail Records) in criminal trials?
response: Call Detail Records (CDRs) are computer-generated secondary evidence of communication between mobile subscribers. Under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, as conclusively held in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020), CDRs are inadmissible in evidence unless accompanied by a valid statutory certificate under Section 65B(4) from the authorized cellular service provider certifying the authenticity and proper functioning of the recording server.

instruction: Explain the essential conditions for grant of Bail under Section 37 of the NDPS Act.
response: Section 37 of the NDPS Act imposes stringent twin conditions for granting bail for commercial quantity offences: (1) The Public Prosecutor must be given an opportunity to oppose the bail application; and (2) Where the Public Prosecutor opposes, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. These conditions operate over and above Section 439 CrPC.

instruction: What is the effect of non-joinder of necessary parties under Order I Rule 9 CPC?
response: Order I Rule 9 CPC provides that no suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties. However, the proviso explicitly clarifies that this protection does not apply to non-joinder of a 'necessary party' (a party in whose absence no effective decree can be passed at all). While non-joinder of a proper party is curable, non-joinder of a necessary party is fatal to the maintainability of the suit.

instruction: What are the rules regarding presumption of legitimate child under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act?
response: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act provides that the birth of a child during the continuance of a valid marriage between mother and any man, or within 280 days after its dissolution, the mother remaining unmarried, is 'conclusive proof' that the child is legitimate. This presumption can be rebutted only by proving that the parties had 'no access' to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. DNA testing is not directed routinely unless a strong prima facie case of non-access is established.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Substituted Performance' under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act (post-2018 amendment).
response: Following the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018, Section 20 was substituted to provide for 'substituted performance'. Where a contract is broken due to non-performance, the suffering party has the option of getting the contract performed by a third party or by their own agency, and recovering the expenses and costs actually incurred from the party in breach, after giving a prior written notice of not less than 30 days.

instruction: Draft a formal Prayer Clause for a Petition under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 for Restitution of Conjugal Rights.
What is the holding in Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012) regarding quashing of non-compoundable offences?
response: In Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012) 10 SCC 303, the Supreme Court held that the High Court has inherent power under Section 482 CrPC to quash criminal proceedings in non-compoundable offences where the parties have settled their private disputes amicably. However, this power must be exercised with caution: Heinous offences like murder, rape, dacoity, economic corruption, or offences against society cannot be quashed on settlement. Disputes of civil, commercial, partnership, or matrimonial nature having personal character can be quashed to secure the ends of justice.

instruction: What is the test of 'Preponderance of Probabilities' versus 'Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt' in Indian Law?
response: In Indian criminal law, the prosecution must establish the guilt of the accused 'beyond reasonable doubt' (higher standard). In civil proceedings and in establishing statutory rebuttals by the accused (such as under Section 139 NI Act or general exceptions in IPC), the standard of proof is 'preponderance of probabilities'. As held in M.S. Narayana Menon v. State of Kerala (2006), the accused is not required to establish their defence beyond doubt; it is sufficient if they raise a probable defence that makes their version believable to a prudent person.

instruction: What are the consequences of an unregistered document requiring compulsory registration under Section 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908?
response: Under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, non-testamentary instruments which create, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest in immovable property of value exceeding one hundred rupees must be compulsorily registered. Under Section 49, an unregistered document requiring compulsory registration cannot affect the immovable property or be received in evidence of any transaction affecting such property. However, the proviso permits its admission as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance under Specific Relief Act, or as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Anticipatory Breach of Contract' under Section 39 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
response: Section 39 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides for Anticipatory Breach of Contract. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety before the due date of performance, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Upon treating the contract as repudiated, the promisee can immediately sue for damages without waiting for the appointed date of performance.

instruction: What is the principle of 'Dominus Litis' in Civil Procedure Code under Order I Rule 10 CPC?
response: The doctrine of 'Dominus Litis' ('master of the suit') establishes that the plaintiff is the master of their litigation and possesses the prerogative to choose against whom they seek relief; the plaintiff cannot be compelled to fight against a party against whom they seek no relief. However, under Order I Rule 10(2) CPC, the court possesses overriding judicial discretion to implead any person as a defendant if their presence is necessary to effectively and completely adjudicate all questions involved in the suit.

instruction: What are the essential conditions for awarding compensation under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?
response: Under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, to claim compensation before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT): (1) The accident must have arisen out of the use of a motor vehicle; (2) The claimant must establish rash and negligent driving on the part of the driver on a preponderance of probabilities; (3) Multiplier method as settled in Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) and National Insurance Co. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) applies for computing loss of dependency, adding future prospects (40% for age below 40 years, 25% for 40-50 years, 10% for 50-60 years), and statutory conventional heads (loss of estate, loss of consortium, funeral expenses).

instruction: What is the distinction between Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder (Section 299 IPC) and Murder (Section 300 IPC) as clarified in State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (1976)?
response: In State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (1976) 4 SCC 382, the Supreme Court mapped the three-stage hierarchy of homicide: All murders are culpable homicide, but not all culpable homicides are murder. The distinction hinges upon the degree of probability of death: Section 299(b) requires bodily injury 'likely' to cause death; Section 300(3) requires bodily injury 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature' to cause death (a higher degree of certainty). If bodily injury is intentionally inflicted and is objectively sufficient in nature to cause death, it falls under Section 300(3) unless covered by the five exceptions.

instruction: Draft a formal Prayer Clause for a Criminal Appeal under Section 374(2) CrPC against conviction.
What is the holding in Lalita Kumari regarding action against police officers for non-registration of FIR?
response: In Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1, the Constitution Bench held that police officers cannot avoid their statutory duty under Section 154 CrPC to register an FIR upon receiving information disclosing a cognizable offence. The Court explicitly mandated that any police officer who fails or refuses to register an FIR in a cognizable case is liable to departmental disciplinary proceedings as well as prosecution for contempt of court, in addition to liability under Section 166A IPC.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 311A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 regarding specimen signatures?
response: Section 311A CrPC empowers a Magistrate of the first class to direct any person, including an accused person, to give specimen signatures or handwriting for the purposes of any investigation or proceeding under the Code. The proviso mandates that no order shall be made under this section unless the person has at some time been arrested in connection with such investigation or proceeding. Such direction does not violate Article 20(3) as held in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Reverse Burden of Proof' under Section 113A and 113B of the Indian Evidence Act.
response: Under Section 113A IEA, when a woman commits suicide within seven years of marriage and it is shown that her husband or his relative subjected her to cruelty, the court 'may presume' abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC (discretionary presumption). Under Section 113B IEA, when the death of a woman is caused by burns or bodily injury within seven years of marriage and it is shown that soon before death she was subjected to cruelty for dowry demand, the court 'shall presume' dowry death under Section 304B IPC (mandatory statutory presumption).

instruction: What are the essential grounds for revocation of a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration under Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
response: Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act provides that the grant of probate or letters of administration may be revoked or annulled for 'just cause'. Just cause is established where: (a) proceedings to obtain grant were defective in substance; (b) grant was obtained fraudulently by making a false suggestion or concealing something material; (c) grant was obtained by means of an untrue allegation of an essential fact; (d) grant has become useless and inoperative through circumstances; (e) person failed to exhibit inventory or accounts.

instruction: Draft a formal Prayer Clause for an Application under Section 340 CrPC for initiating perjury proceedings.
What is the holding in State of M.P. v. Madanlal (2015) regarding compromise in rape cases?
response: In State of M.P. v. Madanlal (2015) 7 SCC 681, the Supreme Court unequivocally ruled that compromise or settlement in cases of rape and sexual assault against women cannot be accepted or acted upon by courts. Rape is a non-compoundable heinous crime against society and human dignity, and courts cannot enter into mediation or quash proceedings based on marriage compromises or monetary settlements.

instruction: What are the essential ingredients of Criminal Trespass under Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Under Section 441 IPC, Criminal Trespass requires: (1) Entry into or upon property in the possession of another; (2) Such entry must be with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy any person in possession; or (3) Having lawfully entered, unlawfully remaining there with such intent. Mere civil trespass without criminal intent does not constitute an offence under Section 441.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Doctrine of Severability' under Article 13 of the Constitution of India.
response: In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) and R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957), the Supreme Court laid down the Doctrine of Severability. If a statute contains provisions that violate Fundamental Rights, the entire Act is not struck down if the invalid part can be cleanly severed from the valid part without affecting the legislative intent. If the valid and invalid parts are so inextricably interwoven that they cannot be separated, the entire statute is invalid.

instruction: Draft a formal Prayer Clause for a Criminal Miscellaneous Petition under Section 439(2) CrPC for Cancellation of Bail.
What is the effect of an order under Section 156(3) CrPC on police investigation as settled in Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P. (2008)?
response: In Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P. (2008) 2 SCC 409, the Supreme Court held that Section 156(3) CrPC is an effective statutory remedy for an aggrieved person when police refuse to register an FIR under Section 154. The Magistrate not only has power to order registration of FIR and investigation, but also possesses incidental powers to monitor the investigation to ensure it is conducted properly and expeditiously, without interfering with the day-to-day work of the investigator.

instruction: What is the difference between Section 397 (Revision) and Section 482 (Inherent Powers) of the CrPC?
response: Section 397 CrPC is a supervisory revisional jurisdiction exercised by the High Court and Sessions Court to examine the correctness, legality, or propriety of any finding, sentence, or order, and is expressly barred against interlocutory orders by Section 397(2). Section 482 CrPC is the inherent power vested exclusively in the High Court to prevent abuse of the process of any court and secure the ends of justice, uninhibited by Section 397(2) in cases of exceptional injustice.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 regarding the statutory cooling-off period of six months as settled in Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017)?
response: In Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746, the Supreme Court held that the six-month statutory waiting period between the first and second motion under Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act is directory and not mandatory. The family court has the discretion to waive the statutory cooling-off period where the parties have settled all disputes, lived apart for more than a year, all efforts at mediation have failed, and waiting further would only prolong their agony.

instruction: What are the ingredients of the offence of Stalking under Section 354D of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Section 354D IPC penalizes stalking: Any man who: (1) follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact such woman to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest; or (2) monitors the use by a woman of the internet, email, or other electronic communication. It is punishable on first conviction with imprisonment up to three years and fine. It provides statutory exceptions where conduct was pursued for preventing or detecting crime.

instruction: What is the distinction between 'Void' and 'Voidable' Marriages under Sections 11 and 12 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?
response: A void marriage (Section 11) is void ab initio from its inception on grounds of bigamy (S. 5(i)), prohibited degree of relationship (S. 5(iv)), or sapinda relationship (S. 5(v)); no decree is legally necessary, though a decree of nullity may be obtained. A voidable marriage (Section 12) is valid and binding until annulled by a decree of nullity on grounds such as impotency (S. 12(1)(a)), unsoundness of mind (S. 12(1)(b)), consent obtained by force or fraud (S. 12(1)(c)), or pre-marriage pregnancy by another (S. 12(1)(d)).

instruction: What is the evidentiary value of an FIR under Section 154 CrPC in a criminal trial?
response: An First Information Report (FIR) is not substantive evidence. It is a previous statement in writing that can only be used under Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act to corroborate the testimony of the maker, or under Section 145 of the Evidence Act to contradict the maker. It cannot be used to contradict or corroborate any other witness who is not the informant, nor can it be used as substantive evidence against the accused.

instruction: What are the essentials of Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 regarding the effect of non-registration of firms?
response: Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act creates statutory disabilities for unregistered firms: (1) No suit to enforce a right arising from contract can be instituted in any court by or on behalf of any person suing as a partner against the firm or other partners unless the firm is registered; (2) No suit to enforce a contractual right can be instituted against any third party by the firm unless registered; (3) No claim of set-off or other proceeding to enforce a contractual right can be maintained. It does not affect the right of third parties to sue the unregistered firm.

instruction: What is the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (Strict Liability) and its modification to Absolute Liability in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987)?
response: The English rule in Rylands v. Fletcher imposed Strict Liability for non-natural use of land subject to exceptions (act of God, plaintiff's consent, third-party act). In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case, 1987 1 SCC 395), the Supreme Court propounded the Indian doctrine of 'Absolute Liability': An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community that no harm shall be caused. The enterprise cannot plead any of the exceptions of strict liability, and damages are measured by the capacity of the enterprise.

instruction: Draft a formal Prayer Clause for a Criminal Appeal under Section 378(4) CrPC against an order of acquittal in a Section 138 NI Act case.
What is the requirement of 'Reason to Believe' under Section 26 of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Section 26 IPC defines 'Reason to Believe': A person is said to have 'reason to believe' a thing, if they have sufficient cause to believe that thing but not otherwise. It requires a higher threshold than mere suspicion or doubt; it contemplates the presence of objective facts that would cause a reasonable, prudent person placed in the same circumstances to arrive at that conclusion.

instruction: What are the rules regarding Inherent Powers under Section 482 BNSS compared to Section 482 CrPC?
response: Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) retains the identical text and substance of Section 482 of the CrPC, 1973. It preserves the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Sanhita, to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. All foundational principles established in Bhajan Lal and Gian Singh continue to apply with full vigor under the new procedural code.
